ALTERNATIVE WORKWEEK SCHEDULE ELECTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Corp

ALTERNATIVE WORKWEEK SCHEDULE ELECTION NOTICE AND DISCLOSURE
Acme Corp proposes to adopt the following alternative workweek schedule, for the work unit described below, under the election procedure described in this information sheet.

Work unit: the Assembly Department

Proposed schedule: four 10-hour days, Monday through Thursday

This notice discloses the effects of the proposed schedule on the affected employees' wages, hours, and benefits. A meeting to discuss those effects will be held on September 15, 2026. A secret ballot election on this proposal is scheduled for September 29, 2026, to be held during regular working hours at the affected employees' work site. Employees who do not attend the meeting will be mailed a copy of this disclosure.

ADOPTING AN ALTERNATIVE WORKWEEK SCHEDULE: THE TWO-THIRDS SECRET-BALLOT VOTE
California law lets the employees within a readily identifiable work unit adopt a regularly scheduled alternative workweek — for example, four 10-hour days — authorizing work of up to 10 hours a day within a 40-hour workweek without triggering the daily overtime that would otherwise apply to hours beyond eight in a day. A proposed alternative workweek schedule takes effect only if it is approved, before any work is performed under it, by at least two-thirds of the affected employees in the work unit, voting in a secret ballot election.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A proposal to adopt an alternative workweek schedule shall be deemed adopted only if it receives approval in a secret ballot election by at least two-thirds of affected employees in a readily identifiable work unit."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 511(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, alternative workweek schedule adoption and vote threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=511.)
  "In order to be valid, the proposed alternative workweek schedule must be adopted in a secret ballot election, before the performance of work, by at least a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the affected employees in the work unit. The election shall be held during regular working hours at the employees’ work site."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(2), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(2) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation; most states have no equivalent alternative-workweek election mechanism at all, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act has no comparable provision. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself adopt, disclose, conduct, certify, or repeal any alternative workweek schedule, and it does not determine that any specific work unit, proposed schedule, disclosure, election, or repeal petition described using this document actually satisfies Labor Code section 511 or the applicable IWC Wage Order. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory and regulatory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session. The two citations below are independent sources corroborating the same rule: Labor Code section 511(a) is the statute, and IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(2), is the Industrial Welfare Commission's regulatory election-procedure text implementing it — a different, independently promulgated source, not a subsection of the same document. Wage Order 4-2001 was fetched as the representative order for this research; Labor Code section 511(f) identifies Wage Order Numbers 1, 4, 5, 7, and 9 as the orders under which alternative workweek schedules can be adopted, and this clause does not independently verify that the other four orders phrase the election-procedure text identically to Wage Order 4, though the statute itself (section 511(a)-(b)) states the core two-thirds vote and overtime rule directly and is not order-specific.

WHAT COUNTS AS A "WORK UNIT"
The vote to adopt or repeal an alternative workweek schedule is taken separately within each readily identifiable work unit, not on a company-wide basis. A work unit can be a division, a department, a job classification, a shift, a separate physical location, or a recognized subdivision of any of those — and, as long as the criteria for an identifiable work unit are otherwise met, a work unit can consist of a single employee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "For purposes of this section, “work unit” includes a division, a department, a job classification, a shift, a separate physical location, or a recognized subdivision thereof. A work unit may consist of an individual employee as long as the criteria for an identifiable work unit in this section is met."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 511(i) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "work unit" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=511.)
  "“affected employees in the work unit” may include all employees in a readily identifiable work unit, such as a division, a department, a job classification, a shift, a separate physical location, or a recognized subdivision of any such work unit. A work unit may consist of an individual employee as long as the criteria for an identifiable work unit in this subsection are met."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(2), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(2) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)

No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory and regulatory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session. The two citations below are independent sources: Labor Code section 511(i) is the statutory definition, and IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(2), is the Industrial Welfare Commission's separately promulgated election-procedure text, which states the same list of examples in near-identical wording. Neither source gives a general test for when a proposed work unit is "readily identifiable" beyond the listed examples, and this clause does not resolve whether any particular grouping of employees would qualify.

WHAT AN ADOPTED ALTERNATIVE WORKWEEK SCHEDULE CHANGES ABOUT OVERTIME
Adopting an alternative workweek schedule does not eliminate overtime; it changes when daily overtime starts. Within the regularly scheduled hours the alternative workweek agreement sets for a scheduled workday — up to 10 hours — those hours are not paid as daily overtime. Hours worked beyond the regularly scheduled hours on a scheduled day, up to 12 hours in that day, and any hours worked beyond 40 in the workweek, are paid at one and one-half times the regular rate. Hours worked beyond 12 in a day, and any hours worked on a day the alternative workweek schedule did not schedule the employee to work at all, are paid at double the regular rate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the employees of an employer may adopt a regularly scheduled alternative workweek that authorizes work by the affected employees for no longer than 10 hours per day within a 40-hour workweek without the payment to the affected employees of an overtime rate of compensation pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 511(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, the 10-hour alternative workweek cap (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=511.)
  "An affected employee working longer than eight hours but not more than 12 hours in a day pursuant to an alternative workweek schedule adopted pursuant to this section shall be paid an overtime rate of compensation of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay of the employee for any work in excess of the regularly scheduled hours established by the alternative workweek agreement and for any work in excess of 40 hours per week."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 511(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, overtime for hours beyond the scheduled alternative workweek day (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=511.)
  "All work performed in excess of 12 hours per day and any work in excess of eight (8) hours on those days worked beyond the regularly scheduled number of workdays established by the alternative workweek agreement shall be paid at double the employee’s regular rate of pay."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(B)(1), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(B)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)

The first two citations below (Labor Code section 511, subdivisions (a) and (b)) are two subdivisions of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not independent corroboration of each other. The third citation, IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(B)(1), is an independent source — a separately promulgated regulation — and is the specific textual basis for the double-time-for-unscheduled-day-work rule stated in the last sentence above, which is present in the wage order's text in materially the same terms as the statute's own subdivision (b) but is quoted from the wage order here because its unscheduled-day framing is clearer there.

REQUIRED PRE-ELECTION DISCLOSURE AND HOW THE VOTE MUST BE CONDUCTED
Before any secret ballot vote on a proposed alternative workweek schedule, the employer must give affected employees a written disclosure describing the proposed schedule's effects on their wages, hours, and benefits, including at least one duly noticed meeting — held at least 14 days before the vote — for the purpose of discussing those effects. An employer that does not comply with this disclosure requirement forfeits the election: it is null and void. The vote itself, and any later vote to repeal the schedule, must be held at the affected employees' work site during regular working hours, at the employer's expense.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Prior to the secret ballot vote, any employer who proposed to institute an alternative workweek schedule shall have made a disclosure in writing to the affected employees, including the effects of the proposed arrangement on the employees’ wages, hours, and benefits. Such a disclosure shall include meeting(s), duly noticed, held at least 14 days prior to voting, for the specific purpose of discussing the effects of the alternative workweek schedule."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(3), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(3) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  "Failure to comply with this paragraph shall make the election null and void."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(3), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(3) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  "Any election to establish or repeal an alternative workweek schedule shall be held at the work site of the affected employees. The employer shall bear the costs of conducting any election held pursuant to this section."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(4), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(4) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)

All three citations below are to paragraphs (3) and (4) of the same wage-order subsection, IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C) — they are treated as one source describing a single election-procedure scheme, not as independent corroboration of each other. Labor Code section 511 itself does not state these disclosure, notice-timing, or worksite/cost requirements; they exist only in the wage order text, which is why no independent statutory citation is offered alongside them. The wage order also requires the written disclosure to be provided in a non-English language when at least five percent of affected employees primarily speak that language, and requires mailing the disclosure to employees who do not attend the meeting; those details are not quoted here but are part of the same disclosure requirement.

REPORTING ELECTION RESULTS: A REAL DISCREPANCY BETWEEN THE STATUTE AND THE WAGE ORDER
The results of an alternative workweek schedule election must be reported by the employer within 30 days after the results are final. Labor Code section 511 identifies the recipient as the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement. The applicable IWC Wage Order identifies the recipient as the Office of the Director – Research, Department of Industrial Relations, and requires that the report include the final vote tally, the size of the unit, and the nature of the employer's business, as a public document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The results of any election conducted pursuant to this section shall be reported by an employer to the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement within 30 days after the results are final."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 511(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, reporting to the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=511.)
  "The results of any election conducted pursuant to this section shall be reported by the employer to the Office of the Director – Research, Department of Industrial Relations within 30 days after the results are final, and the report of election results shall be a public document."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(6), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(6) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)

This is a genuine, unresolved discrepancy in the primary sources rather than a drafting error on this clause's part: the statute (Labor Code section 511(e)) and the wage order (IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(6)) name two different recipient offices for the same 30-day report. Both are independent sources — a statute and a separately promulgated regulation — and both were independently fetched and verified this session; neither text was altered or reconciled to make them agree, and this clause does not resolve which office actually receives reports in current practice. Note for the reader of this research: the recipient named in the wage order, the "Office of the Director – Research," is the current name for what other guidance sometimes calls the Division of Labor Statistics and Research ("DLSR") — neither name refers to the Employment Development Department ("EDD"), which is a different state agency (it administers unemployment insurance and separate new-hire reporting) with no role in this specific reporting requirement.

REPEAL: A ONE-THIRD PETITION FORCES A NEW VOTE
An adopted alternative workweek schedule is not permanent. Affected employees can force a new secret ballot election to repeal it by a petition signed by at least one-third of the affected employees in the work unit; reversing the schedule then requires the same two-thirds vote used to adopt it. The repeal election must be held within 30 days after the petition is submitted, except that a work unit that already voted — to adopt or to repeal — must generally wait at least 12 months before voting on the schedule again. Separately, an employer may not use the adoption, repeal, or nullification of an alternative workweek schedule as an occasion to reduce an employee's regular hourly pay rate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any type of alternative workweek schedule that is authorized by the Labor Code may be repealed by the affected employees. Upon a petition of one-third (1/3) of the affected employees, a new secret ballot election shall be held and a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the affected employees shall be required to reverse the alternative workweek schedule. The election to repeal the alternative workweek schedule shall be held not more than 30 days after the petition is submitted to the employer, except that the election shall be held not less than 12 months after the date that the same group of employees voted in an election held to adopt or repeal an alternative workweek schedule."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(5), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(5) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  "An employer shall not reduce an employee’s regular rate of hourly pay as a result of the adoption, repeal, or nullification of an alternative workweek schedule."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 511(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, no pay-rate reduction on adoption, repeal, or nullification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=511.)

The repeal mechanics quoted below (petition threshold, election timing, and the 12-month interval) come from a single source, IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(5); Labor Code section 511 itself does not spell out the one-third-petition mechanism in its own text, though section 511(f) separately addresses which pre-2000 alternative workweek schedules survived as a historical matter, a different question this clause does not restate. The wage-reduction protection quoted below, Labor Code section 511(c), is an independent source — the statute, not the wage order — and corroborates that both the statute and the wage order contemplate repeal as a real, live possibility rather than describing the schedule as effectively permanent once adopted. The wage order's text also contains a now-historical exception, for schedules adopted between October 1, 1999 and October 1, 2000, to the 12-month interval; that exception is not restated above because it concerns elections from that specific historical window and is not general-purpose guidance.

ANTI-COERCION AND ANTI-RETALIATION PROTECTION FOR THE VOTE
Employers may not intimidate or coerce employees to vote for or against a proposed alternative workweek schedule, and may not discharge or otherwise discriminate against an employee for expressing an opinion about the proposal or for supporting or opposing its adoption or repeal. An employer remains free to state its own position on the proposal to affected employees; the restriction is on coercion and retaliation against employees, not on the employer speaking.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Employers shall not intimidate or coerce employees to vote either in support of or in opposition to a proposed alternative workweek. No employees shall be discharged or discriminated against for expressing opinions concerning the alternative workweek election or for opposing or supporting its adoption or repeal."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(8), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(8) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)

The protection quoted below exists only in the wage order, IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(8) — a single source, not independently corroborated by statutory text — which also states that a violation is "subject to Labor Code Section 98 et seq.," the Labor Commissioner's general wage-claim enforcement procedure; that cross-reference is not independently traced or quoted here.

THIS IS NOT THE SAME AS AN INDIVIDUAL FLEX-TIME ARRANGEMENT
An alternative workweek schedule adopted through this process is a formal, group-level change to a work unit's regularly scheduled workweek, and it changes when daily overtime is legally owed only if it is established through the statutory two-thirds secret-ballot election described above. An informal arrangement between an employer and a single employee to work a compressed or flexible schedule, reached outside a section 511 election, is a different thing: it does not, by itself, change the point at which daily overtime is owed under California law.

ALTERNATIVE WORKWEEK SCHEDULE ELECTION RESULTS AND CERTIFICATION
Work unit: the Assembly Department

Schedule voted on: four 10-hour days, Monday through Thursday

Election date: September 29, 2026

Number of affected employees eligible to vote: 24
Votes in favor: 18
Votes opposed: 6

The undersigned certifies that this secret ballot election was conducted at the affected employees' work site during regular working hours, and that the vote counts above are the final results of that election.

On behalf of Acme Corp:
Name: Jordan Alex Lee
Signature: _______________
City: San Francisco, California   Date: September 29, 2026

citations.quote: An affected employee working longer than eight hours but not more than 12 hours in a day pursuant to an alternative workweek schedule adopted pursuant to this section shall be paid an overtime rate of compensation of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay of the employee for any work in excess of the regularly scheduled hours established by the alternative workweek agreement and for any work in excess of 40 hours per week.

All work performed in excess of 12 hours per day and any work in excess of eight (8) hours on those days worked beyond the regularly scheduled number of workdays established by the alternative workweek agreement shall be paid at double the employee’s regular rate of pay.

expectedJSON.body: Before any secret ballot vote on a proposed alternative workweek schedule, the employer must give affected employees a written disclosure describing the proposed schedule's effects on their wages, hours, and benefits, including at least one duly noticed meeting — held at least 14 days before the vote — for the purpose of discussing those effects. An employer that does not comply with this disclosure requirement forfeits the election: it is null and void. The vote itself, and any later vote to repeal the schedule, must be held at the affected employees' work site during regular working hours, at the employer's expense.

citations.quote: Prior to the secret ballot vote, any employer who proposed to institute an alternative workweek schedule shall have made a disclosure in writing to the affected employees, including the effects of the proposed arrangement on the employees’ wages, hours, and benefits. Such a disclosure shall include meeting(s), duly noticed, held at least 14 days prior to voting, for the specific purpose of discussing the effects of the alternative workweek schedule.
Failure to comply with this paragraph shall make the election null and void.

Any election to establish or repeal an alternative workweek schedule shall be held at the work site of the affected employees. The employer shall bear the costs of conducting any election held pursuant to this section.

expectedJSON.body: The results of an alternative workweek schedule election must be reported by the employer within 30 days after the results are final. Labor Code section 511 identifies the recipient as the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement. The applicable IWC Wage Order identifies the recipient as the Office of the Director – Research, Department of Industrial Relations, and requires that the report include the final vote tally, the size of the unit, and the nature of the employer's business, as a public document.

expectedJSON.body: An adopted alternative workweek schedule is not permanent. Affected employees can force a new secret ballot election to repeal it by a petition signed by at least one-third of the affected employees in the work unit; reversing the schedule then requires the same two-thirds vote used to adopt it. The repeal election must be held within 30 days after the petition is submitted, except that a work unit that already voted — to adopt or to repeal — must generally wait at least 12 months before voting on the schedule again. Separately, an employer may not use the adoption, repeal, or nullification of an alternative workweek schedule as an occasion to reduce an employee's regular hourly pay rate.

citations.quote: Any type of alternative workweek schedule that is authorized by the Labor Code may be repealed by the affected employees. Upon a petition of one-third (1/3) of the affected employees, a new secret ballot election shall be held and a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the affected employees shall be required to reverse the alternative workweek schedule. The election to repeal the alternative workweek schedule shall be held not more than 30 days after the petition is submitted to the employer, except that the election shall be held not less than 12 months after the date that the same group of employees voted in an election held to adopt or repeal an alternative workweek schedule.

expectedJSON.body: Employers may not intimidate or coerce employees to vote for or against a proposed alternative workweek schedule, and may not discharge or otherwise discriminate against an employee for expressing an opinion about the proposal or for supporting or opposing its adoption or repeal. An employer remains free to state its own position on the proposal to affected employees; the restriction is on coercion and retaliation against employees, not on the employer speaking.

citations.quote: Employers shall not intimidate or coerce employees to vote either in support of or in opposition to a proposed alternative workweek. No employees shall be discharged or discriminated against for expressing opinions concerning the alternative workweek election or for opposing or supporting its adoption or repeal.

expectedJSON.body: An alternative workweek schedule adopted through this process is a formal, group-level change to a work unit's regularly scheduled workweek, and it changes when daily overtime is legally owed only if it is established through the statutory two-thirds secret-ballot election described above. An informal arrangement between an employer and a single employee to work a compressed or flexible schedule, reached outside a section 511 election, is a different thing: it does not, by itself, change the point at which daily overtime is owed under California law.

citations.quote: A proposal to adopt an alternative workweek schedule shall be deemed adopted only if it receives approval in a secret ballot election by at least two-thirds of affected employees in a readily identifiable work unit.

In order to be valid, the proposed alternative workweek schedule must be adopted in a secret ballot election, before the performance of work, by at least a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the affected employees in the work unit. The election shall be held during regular working hours at the employees’ work site.
